title.en: Language work for Somebody's Mother: words in context, idioms with hand, lest and diary writing

text.en: A poem about a boy who helps an old woman cross a busy street teaches us verbs that describe helping, idioms with the word hand, a small word that warns, and the way to write a diary.

keepEnglishTerms: free hand, big hand, hand in hand, hands full
hastened, heeded, stir, lend, piled, offered
lend a hand, get out of hand, try your hand at

text.en:
Words from the poem have simple everyday meanings. Hastened means worked quickly, heeded means paid attention to, stir means move slightly, lend means give support, piled means kept in a heap, and offered can mean came forward to help.
The idiom lend a hand means help somebody. Other idioms use hand too. If a situation gets out of hand it becomes difficult to control, and if you try your hand at something you do something new.
To give somebody a free hand is to allow full freedom to act, and to give somebody a big hand is to applaud. To work hand in hand is to work together, and to have your hands full is to be very busy.
Lest is a conjunction meaning to prevent something bad from happening. You can replace it with just in case, as in 'She showed all the documents lest we doubt her'.
Analogies show a pair relationship: heat is to summer as cold is to winter, and hurt is to injured as old is to aged. Find the relationship first, then apply it to the second pair.
The -ed ending has three sounds. After t or d it is pronounced /id/, as in waited and heeded. After voiceless sounds like p, k and s it is /t/, and after most other sounds it is /d/, as in whispered and offered. An adjective like aged or ragged before a noun uses /id/.
A diary entry is personal. Start with the date and day, then write Dear Diary. Describe the day, whom you helped and the situation, the place and time, how you helped, their reaction and how you felt, and say whether you would do it again.
Review the hand idioms in pairs: compare lending a hand to lend support with working hand in hand as partners, so you never mix up helping someone individually and teaming up together.
Check negative purpose with lest carefully. Because lest already carries a warning meaning 'for fear that', never put 'not' right after lest: write Walk slowly lest you slip, not lest you do not slip.
In solving verbal analogies, test the direction of the relationship before choosing an option. Light is to dark as brave is to timid keeps antonym order intact from left to right.
Test the three -ed sounds on regular past verbs from the unit: helped ends with voiceless /t/, offered ends with voiced /d/, and waited or heeded ends with /id/ after t or d.
Before finishing your diary entry, read it back in the first person to make sure the scene shows sensory details, honest emotion, and what the experience taught you about kindness.

problem.en: Use idioms to complete: (a) The teacher gave the students a free ___ to design the show. (b) When the crowd began to push, the situation got out of ___. (c) After the dance the audience gave the performers a big ___.

text.en: (a) hand: to give a free hand means to allow full freedom.

why.en: Match the idiom to its meaning.

text.en: (b) hand: to get out of hand means to become difficult to control.

why.en: The crowd was hard to control.

text.en: (c) hand: to give a big hand means to applaud.

prompt.en: Explain what 'lest' means and give the three sounds of the -ed ending with one example for each.

requiredIdeas.en: lest means to prevent something bad and can be replaced by just in case
/t/ after voiceless sounds and /d/ after most other sounds: whispered

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking -ed is always pronounced the same way

points.en: Hastened, heeded, stir, lend, piled and offered have everyday meanings.
Idioms with hand: lend a hand, get out of hand, try your hand at, a free hand, a big hand, hand in hand, hands full.
Lest means just in case something bad happens.
